headline: In Montana, Bodnar's backers outspent Alme's. Alme won by 10 points.
dek: Independent Seth Bodnar and the super PACs behind him outspent Republican Kurt Alme's side in Montana's open Senate race, according to counts drawn from FEC filings. Alme still won by about 51,000 votes in a three-way race.
summary: Pro-Bodnar groups outspent Alme's allies, but Republican Kurt Alme won Montana's open Senate seat by 10.6 points.

paras.text: Montana's Senate race was the state's first open U.S. Senate race since 1976 with no incumbent on the general election ballot. On March 4, 2026, incumbent Steve Daines (R) withdrew his candidacy and endorsed Alme, who filed to run the same day. Kurt Alme, a former U.S. attorney, beat Seth Bodnar, the former University of Montana president who ran as an independent, by 232,916 votes to 181,674 in the AP count published by The New York Times. That is a margin of 10.6 points. Democrat Alani Bankhead earned just 12% of the vote. The Watch had not finished reading the FEC data for Montana when this piece was published, so the federal figures below come from filings as reported by others, and each one is attributed.

Based on third-quarter FEC reports, Alme raised $3 million and spent $2.4 million. Bodnar raised $4.9 million and spent $4.3 million. Alme had the party's network behind him. Alme Victory, a joint fundraising committee, showed one $350,000 receipt from Daines' Steve Daines for Montana committee. Most of Bodnar's money came from individuals. Contributions from Montana residents total $1.45 million, which the Glasgow Courier reported was 36.5% of his individual contributions. California donors represented 18.5% of the total.

The outside money tilted further toward Bodnar. Independent PAC, a hybrid PAC, is affiliated with the national Independent Leadership Council. That group was founded in 2026 by former U.S. senator Joe Manchin, his daughter Heather Manchin, former FreedomWorks president Adam Brandon, and former Forbes chief impact officer Seth Cohen. Inside Elections traced a network of pro-Bodnar super PACs, including Montana Freedom PAC, that was paid for partly through Way Back PAC. One donor was computer scientist Scott Shenker, who gave a similar amount to the pro-Bodnar Montana Freedom PAC. In the Democratic primary, Progressive Vet PAC spent $3.3 million promoting Bankhead. Most of Progressive Vet PAC's money came from Contours, Inc., a 501(c)(4) nonprofit organization not required to disclose its donors. That arrangement is what "dark money" means in the legal sense. Inside Elections wrote that all available evidence points to its true candidate being Bodnar.

On Alme's side, Americans for Prosperity Action, a super PAC in the Koch network, has spent more than $2.1 million supporting Alme, the Flathead Beacon reported in October. Its funders include the Koch family and members of the Walton clan, owners of Walmart. The FEC lists More Jobs, Less Government as a hybrid PAC. It had spent $22 million to benefit Republican Tim Sheehy in Montana's 2024 Senate race, and its federal organizing paperwork also lists Daines Senate Majority Fund and Team Alme as joint fundraising representatives.

The totals depend on who is counting. VoteLog, a site that compiles FEC filings, counted outside money benefiting each candidate: Alme $4,053,995 and Bodnar $10,870,738. In mid-October, the Flathead Beacon credited Bodnar with only $134,482.52 in support from Montana Freedom PAC. The Watch could not reconcile the two counts before publication.

Republican money showed up first in the Democratic primary. More Jobs, Less Government ran TV ads saying Neill is "too liberal," and claiming Bankhead is a "conservative Democrat" who agrees with President Donald Trump on immigration. After the primary, the pro-Bodnar Montana Freedom PAC poured money into signs and digital ads suggesting Bankhead should leave the race.

Montana Free Press reported that, according to TV contracts, two Alme-supporting PACs, American Leadership Fund and More Jobs, Less Government, recently placed $750,000 in cable ads against Bodnar. The ads, scheduled to run through the Aug. 10 withdrawal deadline, target Bodnar's tenure as University of Montana president. One of them cited a lawsuit. A fact-check by the station NonStop Local found that in 2021, 18 UM female employees sued the University of Montana, and that it also uses examples of AI generated pictures of Bodnar himself.

Independent PAC's main TV ad went after Alme's record as a prosecutor, saying he declined most of the sex-crime cases his office received. NonStop Local found that Alme's office declined to prosecute 61 out of a total 80 cases of sexual abuse during the 2018, 2019, and 2020 fiscal years, and that the rate was in line with other U.S. attorneys' offices. Alme's campaign said this week that about a third of those cases his office considered were referred to other agencies. The National Republican Senatorial Committee sent a cease-and-desist letter to Montana stations asking them to pull the ad. According to the Montana State News Bureau, the NRSC tried unsuccessfully to get it off the air.

AFP Action's ads sold Alme's biography and his tax record. AFP said one buy will fund targeted digital, streaming, and connected TV advertising. Online spending added up quickly. In one 30-day stretch in the spring, nearly $700,000 has been spent in Montana on Google platforms alone, mostly on the Senate race, the Daily Montanan reported.

By most counts, the side that spent more lost. Alme ran a quiet campaign. Montana Free Press reported that Alme's exposure to voters came largely through events not advertised to the general public, super PACs spent $4 million on ads promoting his candidacy. Alme's 10.6-point margin was about half of Trump's 19.9-point margin in Montana in 2024. With a Democrat also on the ballot, though, the two numbers aren't directly comparable.

Democrats disagree about what Bodnar's money accomplished. Montana Democratic Party executive director Emily Marburger described the "independent experiment" as a failure. Nancy Keenan, a former state party director who backed Bodnar, wrote that he "ran a competitive race that forced the GOP to expend resources in Montana (including millions to prop up Alani Bankhead)". A political scientist cautioned that the calculus of what could have been isn't as easy as combining the vote shares of two candidates.
